language_wrapper: A hallway has {num_lockers} closed lockers labeled 1 through {num_lockers}. A student begins at locker 1 and walks left-to-right. On each left-to-right traversal, he opens the {left_offset}-th closed locker he encounters and then repeats the pattern of skipping {stride_minus_one} closed lockers and opening the next closed locker among the still-closed ones, until he reaches the end. He immediately turns around and walks right-to-left. On each right-to-left traversal, he opens the {right_offset}-th closed locker he encounters and then repeats the same skip-and-open pattern with stride {stride} among the still-closed lockers. He continues traversing back and forth, always using the same offsets ({left_offset} from the left, {right_offset} from the right) and stride {stride}, until every locker is open. What is the number of the last locker he opens?
teacher_generator_code:
def generator(rng):
    # Generate parameters and ensure the instance is nontrivial and requires multiple passes
    # We'll simulate with a Fenwick tree to pre-validate difficulty constraints.

    def bit_build(n):
        return [0] * (n + 1)

    def bit_add(bit, n, i, delta):
        while i <= n:
            bit[i] += delta
            i += i & -i

    def bit_sum(bit, i):
        s = 0
        while i > 0:
            s += bit[i]
            i -= i & -i
        return s

    def bit_select(bit, n, k):
        # Find smallest index i with prefix sum >= k
        if k <= 0:
            return None
        total = bit_sum(bit, n)
        if k > total:
            return None
        idx = 0
        # Largest power of two >= n
        bitmask = 1 << (n.bit_length())
        while bitmask > n:
            bitmask >>= 1
        while bitmask:
            t = idx + bitmask
            if t <= n and bit[t] < k:
                idx = t
                k -= bit[t]
            bitmask >>= 1
        return idx + 1

    def simulate(n, stride, left_offset, right_offset):
        # Returns (last_opened, num_passes)
        bit = bit_build(n)
        for i in range(1, n + 1):
            bit_add(bit, n, i, 1)
        m = n
        last = None
        num_passes = 0
        # Alternate passes: left, right, left, right, ... until all are opened
        left_turn = True
        while m > 0:
            if left_turn:
                r = left_offset
                performed = False
                while r is not None and r <= m and m > 0:
                    pos = bit_select(bit, n, r)
                    if pos is None:
                        break
                    bit_add(bit, n, pos, -1)
                    m -= 1
                    last = pos
                    performed = True
                    r += (stride - 1)
                if performed:
                    num_passes += 1
                left_turn = False
            else:
                # Right-to-left pass
                # First target is the right_offset-th closed from the right => left-based rank = m - right_offset + 1
                r = m - right_offset + 1
                performed = False
                while r is not None and r >= 1 and m > 0:
                    pos = bit_select(bit, n, r)
                    if pos is None:
                        break
                    bit_add(bit, n, pos, -1)
                    m -= 1
                    last = pos
                    performed = True
                    r -= (stride - 1)
                if performed:
                    num_passes += 1
                left_turn = True
        return last, num_passes

    def is_power_of_two(x):
        return x > 0 and (x & (x - 1)) == 0

    for _ in range(200):
        n = rng.randint(600, 20000)
        stride = rng.randint(2, min(40, n))
        left_offset = rng.randint(1, stride)
        right_offset = rng.randint(1, stride)
        # Avoid trivial symmetric cases occasionally
        if stride == 2 and is_power_of_two(n):
            continue
        last, passes = simulate(n, stride, left_offset, right_offset)
        # Enforce nontrivial instance: multiple passes and last is not at ends
        if last is None:
            continue
        if passes < 3:
            continue
        if last in (1, n):
            continue
        return {
            'num_lockers': n,
            'stride': stride,
            'left_offset': left_offset,
            'right_offset': right_offset,
            'stride_minus_one': stride - 1
        }

    # Fallback: choose a safe parameter set
    n = 1500
    stride = 3
    left_offset = 1
    right_offset = 2
    return {
        'num_lockers': n,
        'stride': stride,
        'left_offset': left_offset,
        'right_offset': right_offset,
        'stride_minus_one': stride - 1
    }
hardness_rationale: This family generalizes the seed’s bidirectional every-other opening into a bidirectional, offset-sensitive, stride-s elimination among still-closed lockers. The direction-dependent offsets (left_offset and right_offset) and general stride require tracking the order of openings across alternating passes, which no longer collapses to the classical elimination-game closed form for stride 2. Solving an instance typically needs an order-statistics or affine-mapping approach to model successive removals, or a data structure (e.g., a Fenwick tree) to simulate efficiently—guessing or simple parity arguments are insufficient. The verifier enforces multiple passes and non-endpoint answers, preventing trivial cases.
notes: Proof sketch of correctness: Model the process on the set {1,2,...,n} of closed lockers, with an element present (closed) or removed (opened). On a left-to-right pass with stride s and offset t, the openings occur at ranks r = t, t + s, t + 2s, ... among the current closed set. After removing at rank r, the next target is r + (s − 1) because one item has been removed; skipping exactly s − 1 closed lockers moves the next opening to the previous rank plus s − 1 in the updated list. On a right-to-left pass with stride s and offset t, the first opening is the t-th from the right, i.e., left-based rank r = m − t + 1 if m is the current number of closed lockers. Subsequent openings decrease the left-based rank by (s − 1) for the same reason: after each removal, among the remaining m − 1 lockers, skipping s − 1 from the right moves the target left by s − 1 ranks. A Fenwick tree maintains the set of closed lockers and provides: (i) O(log n) updates to open a locker, and (ii) an O(log n) order-statistics query to select the locker at a given rank among the closed ones, via a standard prefix-sum search. Alternating these pass rules until all lockers are opened yields a unique sequence of openings; the last element opened is exactly the last removal under this deterministic process. For stride s = 2 and offsets t = 1, this reduces to the classical elimination game whose survivor (if one stops early) is known to be 342 for n = 1024; continuing to open the survivor last matches the seed. For general s and offsets, the rank-update invariants (±(s − 1) per removal on each pass) ensure the simulation matches the stated process and thus returns the correct last-opened locker. The verifier also enforces nontrivial instances (≥ 3 passes, non-endpoint answer) to preserve difficulty.
source_question: A bored student walks down a hall that contains a row of closed lockers, numbered 1 to 1024. He opens the locker numbered 1, and then alternates between skipping and opening each locker thereafter. When he reaches the end of the hall, the student turns around and starts back. He opens the first closed locker he encounters, and then alternates between skipping and opening each closed locker thereafter. The student continues wandering back and forth in this manner until every locker is open. What is the number of the last locker he opens?
